annotation_description: Bottoming Ocelot Pride leaves the hand with 4 lands and only 2 threats (Ragavan + Seasoned Pyromancer), making the hand land-heavy for an aggressive deck. Ocelot Pride is a strong 1-drop with lifelink that triggers its own token generation, and pairs well alongside Ragavan for early pressure.

Fetching a basic Mountain instead of Sacred Foundry or Elegant Parlor is suboptimal. The player already has two Plains in hand, so white mana is covered. However, fetching Sacred Foundry (paying 2 life to have it enter untapped) would provide both red and white mana from a single land, giving more flexibility in future turns. More importantly, the player has Seasoned Pyromancer (1RR) in hand which needs double red - having a Sacred Foundry that can produce either color keeps options open for casting both Ragavan now and Seasoned Pyromancer later when combined with other lands. A basic Mountain only produces red, while Sacred Foundry produces both. Since the hand already has two Plains, color flexibility from the land base is valuable. That said, fetching a basic Mountain does dodge potential Blood Moon effects and saves 2 life, so this is a minor optimization issue rather than a major mistake.

message: You may choose an alternative cost
annotation_description: On turn 1 with only one Mountain available, casting Ragavan for {R} uses the entire mana for the turn, which is fine. However, the decision to hard-cast rather than Dash is worth examining. The hand contains Flooded Strand, Plains, Plains, and Seasoned Pyromancer - no removal protection and no way to cast Seasoned Pyromancer until turn 3 at earliest. Hard-casting Ragavan on turn 1 is generally correct as it can start generating value earlier and applies pressure. However, against an unknown opponent's deck that could have Lightning Bolt, Fatal Push, or other cheap removal, there's a risk of losing the card entirely. With Dash, Ragavan would return to hand if it connects or if the opponent removes it before combat. That said, the conventional wisdom is that turn 1 hard-cast Ragavan is correct in most scenarios since the tempo advantage of having it stick is enormous, and you want it to survive to attack on future turns without re-investing mana. This is likely correct but debatable.

Playing Sunbaked Canyon on turn 1 when there's no turn 1 spell to cast means paying unnecessary life on future taps. Against an aggressive opponent with Ragavan already on board, life total preservation matters. A fetchland or basic Mountain would provide mana without repeated life costs.

Playing Plains instead of Flooded Strand is slightly suboptimal. Flooded Strand is a fetchland that can find Plains or Island, providing deck thinning and flexibility. Since the player has two Plains in hand already, playing the Flooded Strand now preserves the option to play Plains later while getting the same mana access. Additionally, with Seasoned Pyromancer in hand (costs 1RR), the player needs red mana more than white, and Flooded Strand can't fetch Mountains anyway - but it still thins the deck. However, the more important consideration is that Flooded Strand should be played before Plains to maintain flexibility in future turns, as the Plains can always be played later but the fetchland provides strictly more options when played first.

chosen_display: Glimpse the Impossible — Cast Glimpse the Impossible [Activate]
annotation_description: Cast Glimpse the Impossible instead of Seasoned Pyromancer. Seasoned Pyromancer was castable (Mountain + Plains + Treasure = {1}{R}{R}) and would have been significantly stronger here - putting a 2/2 body on board, discarding the dead duplicate Ragavan and a land, drawing 2 fresh cards, and creating 1-2 elemental tokens. The hand had perfect discard fodder.

Playing Scalding Tarn instead of Mountain costs 1 unnecessary life to fetch a Mountain, when a Mountain is already in hand. Both achieve the same result of having 2 mana for Ruby Medallion this turn. The fetchland should be saved for later when deck thinning/shuffling is more valuable or when no basics are available.

chosen_display: Sunbaked Canyon — {1}, {T}, Sacrifice {this}: Draw a card. [Activate]
annotation_description: Sacrificing Sunbaked Canyon to draw a card instead of fetching with Scalding Tarn loses a mana source unnecessarily. Fetching with Scalding Tarn would preserve Sunbaked Canyon as both a mana source and a future card draw option, while still enabling Ruby Medallion this turn.

Blood Moon is terrible against a mono-red opponent. It does virtually nothing to them (turns Sunbaked Canyon into a slightly better Mountain) while actively hurting Timmy's own white mana access from future nonbasic lands like Flooded Strand. Casting it required sacrificing 2 Eldrazi Spawn tokens for mana, wasting those resources on an enchantment that hurts the caster more than the opponent.

Playing Flooded Strand instead of Plains is suboptimal when planning to cast Blood Moon. Under Blood Moon, Flooded Strand becomes a Mountain (redundant red source), while a basic Plains would be unaffected and preserve white mana access. If they crack Flooded Strand for a Plains, they lose 1 life unnecessarily for the same result as just playing Plains directly.

chosen_display: Flooded Strand — {T}, Pay 1 life, Sacrifice {this}: Search your li... [Activate]
annotation_description: Cracking Flooded Strand before combat with Ragavan is a sequencing error. Ragavan's combat damage trigger exiles a card from the opponent's library that can be cast this turn and creates a Treasure token. Seeing that card first could inform whether to fetch Plains or Island, and the Treasure provides additional mana. Additionally, the opponent's lands are tapped, so there's no combat trick risk.

annotation_description: Blood Moon is an extremely powerful card against the opponent who is playing with nonbasic lands (Sunbaked Canyon is currently on their battlefield and would become a basic Mountain under Blood Moon, losing its card-draw ability). The opponent's deck likely relies on nonbasic lands. Discarding Blood Moon to Seasoned Pyromancer wastes a high-impact card. Since one of the two discards must be a nonland card to generate an Elemental token, discarding Ragavan (which is a nonland) would generate a token AND preserve Blood Moon for casting next turn. The player already has a Ragavan on the battlefield, so the second copy is legendary and much less valuable. Blood Moon could have been cast as early as next turn with the mana available (3 lands + Eldrazi Spawn tokens for colorless).

The player chose to attack with only Ragavan when they also had three Eldrazi Spawn tokens (0/1) and Seasoned Pyromancer (2/2) available. The opponent has no untapped creatures to block. Attacking with all creatures would deal 2 (Ragavan) + 2 (Pyromancer) + 0+0+0 (Spawn tokens) = 4 damage instead of just 2. The Spawn tokens deal 0 damage but could still attack safely since there are no blockers. However, the player's reasoning about preserving Spawn tokens as mana sources has some merit - they could sacrifice them for 3 colorless mana on a future turn. The Seasoned Pyromancer attacking for 2 extra damage with no risk of being blocked is clearly correct though. At minimum, Seasoned Pyromancer should have been sent in alongside Ragavan for 2 additional free damage.

Blood Moon does almost nothing against the opponent who is playing a mono-red strategy with Ruby Medallion and basic Mountains. Their only nonbasic (Sunbaked Canyon) actually benefits from becoming a pain-free Mountain. Meanwhile, Blood Moon cuts off Timmy's own white mana from Sacred Foundry and prevents Dalkovan Encampment from being useful, losing access to white spells and the token-generating ability.

Blood Moon is nearly useless against the opponent who is essentially mono-red (only nonbasic is Sunbaked Canyon). Meanwhile, it hurts Timmy by turning Sacred Foundry into a plain Mountain (losing white), making Flooded Strand enter as a tapped Mountain instead of fetching, and neutering Dalkovan Encampment's activated ability. Spending 3 mana and a card to minimally impact the opponent while degrading your own mana base is a significant waste.

Blood Moon turns all nonbasic lands into Mountains. Gem25F Timmy controls Sacred Foundry (nonbasic) which is their only source of white mana. Casting Blood Moon removes their own access to white mana, shutting off Dalkovan Encampment's white abilities and any future white spells. Additionally, Flooded Strand in hand becomes useless (it would be a Mountain that can only tap for R, and its search ability is replaced). The opponent (MiniMx Truth) only has Sunbaked Canyon as a nonbasic land alongside two basic Mountains - Sunbaked Canyon becoming a Mountain is a minor inconvenience but the opponent is already heavily red-based. Meanwhile, Timmy's own board and hand are significantly hurt: Sacred Foundry loses white production, Flooded Strand becomes a tapless Mountain (actually it enters as a Mountain with no fetch ability), and Dalkovan Encampment becomes a Mountain losing its token-creating ability. The self-damage outweighs the disruption to the opponent.

Casting Ragavan before combat and before playing a land is a sequencing error. Ragavan is a legendary creature, and the player already has one on the battlefield - casting a second copy will cause the legend rule to force sacrificing one of them. This wastes the card entirely. Even if the intent was to replace the existing Ragavan (which makes no sense), this is a wasted card. Additionally, even if it were legal/useful, casting creatures before combat when you could attack first is generally suboptimal, and playing a land (Flooded Strand or Dalkovan Encampment) before casting spells is better sequencing.

Dalkovan Encampment enters untapped (controls a Mountain) and has an activated ability ({2}{W}, {T}) that creates two 1/1 attacking Warriors. With 3 Eldrazi Spawn tokens available to sacrifice for colorless mana, the player could activate this ability (sac 2 Spawn + tap Encampment) to create 2 extra attacking creatures, dealing significantly more combat damage. Flooded Strand just fetches a basic Plains at the cost of 1 life, providing the same mana but without the combat ability.

Cast Reckless Impulse before playing a land. With two Wooded Foothills in hand, playing one first (and potentially cracking it for a Mountain) would provide an additional mana to cast whatever cards are exiled by Reckless Impulse. At 7 life against an opponent with creatures, maximizing the ability to use exiled cards this turn is important.

With Manamorphose available from exile (via Artist's Talent), casting it before Wrenn's Resolve would be better sequencing. Manamorphose with Ruby Medallion costs {1} and produces 2 mana of any color plus draws a card - it's mana-positive and provides information before committing to additional card-draw spells. This extra mana and card could meaningfully affect the combo turn's success.

Cast Wish before playing a land drop. Wooded Foothills could have been played for free first, then cracked for a Mountain to provide additional mana for later plays this combo turn. Since they're at 7 life and in the middle of a combo turn with all lands tapped, every point of mana matters.

Casting Past in Flames flashback first uses all available mana, leaving no mana to actually flashback any of the rituals and spells in the graveyard. Past in Flames only gives flashback until end of turn, so the mana needs to be available after it resolves.

At 2 life facing lethal on board next turn (Ragavan + Seasoned Pyromancer + Eldrazi Spawn tokens), MiniMx Truth cast Artist's Talent, a slow value enchantment, instead of attempting to combo off with Past in Flames flashback chains. With Ruby Medallion reducing costs and multiple Pyretic Rituals, Manamorphoses, and Reckless Impulses available for flashback, they had a potential storm/burn kill line. Artist's Talent does nothing to prevent dying next combat.

The opponent is at 2 life. Gem25F Timmy has Galvanic Discharge in hand, which gives 3 energy counters and can deal damage to a creature or planeswalker - but critically, it cannot target players directly. However, the real issue is sequencing: Ocelot Pride is being cast pre-combat instead of after combat. Gem25F Timmy has Ragavan (2/1), Seasoned Pyromancer (2/2), Elemental Token (1/1), and three Eldrazi Spawn tokens (0/1 each) on the battlefield. The opponent is at 2 life with all lands tapped and no blockers. Attacking with Ragavan alone deals 2 damage for lethal. By casting Ocelot Pride before combat instead of just attacking, Timmy risks the opponent having some interaction (though all lands are tapped). More importantly, this is a case of not recognizing that lethal is already on board - just attack with Ragavan (2/1) for exactly 2 damage against the opponent at 2 life.
